segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: I appreciate you coming.

segments.speaker: david-sands
segments.translation: Me too.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Let me tell you the reason we are doing this. You know they have a school learning Cherokee here? Children on this side and adults on this side. They are going to start listening, but I don’t know when they are going to start. They are going to start listening to good Cherokee speakers, and also, if you have grandchildren, someday, we both are going to pass on. They might want to hear you talking. They will let them listen to you speak if they come and ask. They will allow them to listen to you talking. As we first begin, tell me your full name in English.

segments.speaker: david-sands
segments.translation: In English? David Sands.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: David Sands. What about in Cherokee?

segments.speaker: david-sands
segments.translation: Dolvtsi, Dolvtsi Noyi.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Dolvtsi Noyi. Where were you born?

segments.speaker: david-sands
segments.translation: I was born in Tahlequah. And where I grew up was Iyo Holler.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Pumpkin Holler?

segments.speaker: david-sands
segments.translation: Pumpkin Holler.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: What was it like where you grew up in Iyo?

segments.speaker: david-sands
segments.translation: There was not very much where I grew up in Pumpkin Holler. I guess, playing on the road without shoes on. Back then, it was not until winter I was given new...

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: You were given?

segments.speaker: david-sands
segments.translation: I was given shoes for the winter.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: How many were in your family?

segments.speaker: david-sands
segments.translation: Wait... there were about eight or nine of us, I think. And a half-brother named Scot Maclemore. There were more of us back then. There are three that I know of that passed away.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: That are not alive. Did all of y’all speak Cherokee?

segments.speaker: david-sands
segments.translation: Back then, when we lived in Pumpkin with Dad and Mom, we all spoke Cherokee. Back then, but when some grew up, they started.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: To speak English?

segments.speaker: david-sands
segments.translation: Yes, speaking English.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: What did your father use to do?

segments.speaker: david-sands
segments.translation: As far as I know, Dad worked on the railroad.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Railroad.

segments.speaker: david-sands
segments.translation: And also, in the beginning, they made ties for the railroad. He just did different things back then. Then he started working on the railroad. He worked a long time there.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Were you not old enough to help him make those ties?

segments.speaker: david-sands
segments.translation: No, I wasn’t. I was just walking around in the woods all the time. My dad and his brother and all of my uncles got together and made ties.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: They made ties. Where did they take them when they were finished?

segments.speaker: david-sands
segments.translation: They would go sell them in Proctor?

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: They would go sell them.

segments.speaker: david-sands
segments.translation: And toward Siloam. If someone had a truck, they would take them to Siloam.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: They would go sell them?

segments.speaker: david-sands
segments.translation: They would sell them.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Back then did y’all not have electricity?

segments.speaker: david-sands
segments.translation: No, really didn’t.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Did y’all just...?

segments.speaker: david-sands
segments.translation: What do they call those?

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Was it coil oil?

segments.speaker: david-sands
segments.translation: Yes.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: What about your house, how big was it?

segments.speaker: david-sands
segments.translation: It was one room, and there were a lot of us living there. Sometimes I think about that, and wonder how we able to rest at night. All of us children, then Mom and Dad and my uncle stayed there. And my grandmother was blind. She lived there, too, my dad’s mother. She was blind, and she lived there, too.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: That is the way it was back then, ain’t it? It was not just family, it was relatives or just anyone, too, could live with you.

segments.speaker: david-sands
segments.translation: Yes, we all just lived in one house. I think about that sometimes. I wonder what we did to get rest at night - all the children and mother, all of us.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Did you go to school?

segments.speaker: david-sands
segments.translation: I started school there in Pumpkin Hollow. They called that school Pumpkin Center. That was where I started going to school, and I was in second grade when we moved from where we lived. I forget the name of the landowner where we lived. He sold it, so we came toward Briggs then. So I grew up in Briggs. I was about 14 or 15 years old when we moved toward Chewy.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Did you not finish school?

segments.speaker: david-sands
segments.translation: No, I didn’t.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Were you able to speak English when you started going to school?

segments.speaker: david-sands
segments.translation: It was all in English, but there were a lot of us Cherokee going to school in Pumpkin Hollow, and toward Briggs it was the same way. Half were white and half were Cherokee. We all went to school for a little while, then we went toward Chewy and then, I did not go to school anymore.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Was it hard for you? Because you probably didn’t speak English.

segments.speaker: david-sands
segments.translation: Not very much English back then. I was learning, though. But it was then that I forgot some Cherokee when I started going to school.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Were y’all scolded when y’all spoke Cherokee?

segments.speaker: david-sands
segments.translation: No, I don’t think so. I didn’t know it was like that. We wanted to speak English. Sometimes we would speak Cherokee when some of us boys would play.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: What about you? How many children do you have?

segments.speaker: david-sands
segments.translation: It was four. I just have three girls now. The boy passed away.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Did they also speak Cherokee?

segments.speaker: david-sands
segments.translation: No, they just know English. That was all they learned at school. They forgot the rest of Cherokee.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Do you still live in Chewy now?

segments.speaker: david-sands
segments.translation: Yes, still there.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Did y’all buy land there?

segments.speaker: david-sands
segments.translation: My wife’s aunt gave us an acre there.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: So y’all still live there.

segments.speaker: david-sands
segments.translation: We were given an Indian home. We still live there.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Do you plant a garden?

segments.speaker: david-sands
segments.translation: What?

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Do you plant a garden?

segments.speaker: david-sands
segments.translation: Sometimes, but this summer nobody...

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Tilled it up for you?

segments.speaker: david-sands
segments.translation: Nobody tilled it up for me. Last year my grandson brought a tractor and tilled it. I planted a little bit, but this time he didn’t have a tractor. I didn’t grow anything this summer, but I do have tomatoes planted. They call them [unclear] they call them. I have nine of those tomato plants planted.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: It has been really hard to plant anything because of the rains.

segments.speaker: david-sands
segments.translation: That’s true, it’s been raining, but I am glad that it rained.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: When you were growing up, you said you were in the woods. Were y’all hunting?

segments.speaker: david-sands
segments.translation: All the time. As for me, it was just being in the woods.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: So, you just liked it?

segments.speaker: david-sands
segments.translation: I was going everywhere in the woods. I had four dogs that followed me, or I was following them in the woods. We were going everywhere.

segments.speaker: michael-cooksey
segments.translation: That big river, you probably have fished in that big river, haven’t you?

segments.speaker: david-sands
segments.translation: No, I really have not fished that much.

segments.speaker: michael-cooksey
segments.translation: You haven’t?

segments.speaker: david-sands
segments.translation: I haven’t fished that much, but my brother and father fished all the time. As for me, I have not fished that much.

segments.speaker: michael-cooksey
segments.translation: They were catching big ones sometimes there?

segments.speaker: david-sands
segments.translation: Yes, what do they call them? Carp. They were catching big ones. Nowadays, they hardly exist. [unclear] was saying they all went toward the lake. You won’t hardly see them anymore, Acorn was saying.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: What about crawdads? Are they in there?

segments.speaker: david-sands
segments.translation: Yes, a few. What they call river otters, they are everywhere now.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Those kind live there?

segments.speaker: david-sands
segments.translation: They eat up the crawdads in the little creeks.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: I didn’t know any were living.

segments.speaker: david-sands
segments.translation: Yes, they are everywhere now.

segments.speaker: michael-cooksey
segments.translation: What about in Cherokee? You said your name was Dolvtsi?

segments.speaker: david-sands
segments.translation: Dolvtsi.

segments.speaker: michael-cooksey
segments.translation: What is the meaning of that? Was that someone’s name that you were given?

segments.speaker: david-sands
segments.translation: Dolvtsi is a tree. A red oak, dolvtsi.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Is that the name of it?

segments.speaker: david-sands
segments.translation: Red oak is dolvtsi.

segments.speaker: michael-cooksey
segments.translation: As far as I know, it is vdaya.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Me too. That was all I knew - vdaya. That is its real name, ain’t it? Dolvtsi.

segments.speaker: david-sands
segments.translation: As far as I know, that is red oak - dolvtsi to me.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: What about when you were growing up? Y’all burned wood, ain’t it?

segments.speaker: david-sands
segments.translation: Yes, that is true.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Did you boys ever help cut it?

segments.speaker: david-sands
segments.translation: Yes, when Dad was not working, every day he would take an axe up the long hollow and cut some down this big [gesture], and gather them up. And on Saturdays, when us boys were not doing anything, we would all go. My dad and my brothers. There were two or three of us brothers, and Grandpa and Dad. We all went. We used a crosscut. Me and Uncle were partners. We would cut one. They would put another one on there, then my dad and my brother would cut one. That is what we did on Saturdays, we would cut wood.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Y’all must have done it pretty quick. What about taking them toward the house? How did y’all take them?

segments.speaker: david-sands
segments.translation: I really don’t know, I guess sometimes... What was the name of that old man? He had a wagon. We would go borrow horses, and we would use that.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Y’all pulled them?

segments.speaker: david-sands
segments.translation: We pulled that wood to the house, and when they made ties... what do they call them? Juggles. We would put them on a horse wagon, and we would take it to the house.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: I rode in one of those one time, the kind of wagon you use horses to pull. When I think about it, I would have liked to have lived back then, I think.

segments.speaker: david-sands
segments.translation: The last time I rode in a wagon in Hulburt. My uncle lived in Rocky Ford. He raised corn. I wondered why he raised corn. He didn’t have hogs or hardly anything. He raised a lot of corn across the creek from his house. It was brown where he raised corn. He bought some mules in Hulburt. I went with him. We came all the way from there in a wagon. We came towards Rocky Ford. We started about eight or nine in the morning, coming toward Rocky Ford. We came by Lost City and Moody. Somewhere, we were using old roads in the woods. I didn’t know, but my uncle knew. At nine o’clock that night, we got to Rocky Ford.

segments.speaker: michael-cooksey
segments.translation: In the evening or at night?

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: At night. That is how long it took?

segments.speaker: david-sands
segments.translation: All day, we were in a wagon. We got to his house in Rocky Ford at nine o’clock at night. Then a week went by, and then he went and picked me up. Then we started picking corn.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Did y’all pick them by hand?

segments.speaker: david-sands
segments.translation: Yes, we were putting them in a corn wagon.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Did y’all just throw them in there?

segments.speaker: david-sands
segments.translation: Yes, in the wagon. He had a big barn we put them in.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Were they already dry?

segments.speaker: david-sands
segments.translation: Yes.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: What did he do with them if he did not have any hogs?

segments.speaker: david-sands
segments.translation: I don’t know, but I had hogs.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: You had some.

segments.speaker: david-sands
segments.translation: It seemed I had about 15 back then. It was open range, and they were outside. He gave me 25 bushels of corn. I used that to feed the hogs that I had. And I built a little fence to put four in, to fatten them up.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: For y’all to kill.

segments.speaker: david-sands
segments.translation: So when they got good enough, Dad said, “Kill two of them hogs.” He said, “As for me, I am going to Tahlequah.” It was then that I started fixing hogs.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: So, when it was open range, they were just everywhere in the woods. What about, say for instance, that if you thought, “I am going to put some in to fatten up.” Did y’all go look for them while they were in the woods?

segments.speaker: david-sands
segments.translation: Yes, they were tame. They were everywhere in the woods. We would go get them, and they would follow us to the house. I would throw corn over the fence, and they would all come in there. I wanted to fatten them up. I had one small, fenced area. I would put them in there. Those hogs were tame.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Did any of your neighbors have hogs, too?

segments.speaker: david-sands
segments.translation: Yes, those hogs lived everywhere in the woods.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Did y’all know them? Did y’all clip their ears?

segments.speaker: david-sands
segments.translation: Yes.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Yes, OK. That was how you recognized them.

segments.speaker: david-sands
segments.translation: They ‘cut their ears off,’ they called it. We put a V, and others were different, and some would cut the tail off a little bit, so they would know it was theirs, and we would know what was ours. And if they belonged to someone else, we would know them.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Did you sell some of them?

segments.speaker: david-sands
segments.translation: Sometimes we would sell them. There was a man named Hampton that lived there. He was a farmer. He gave me three of them this big [gesture].

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: That big.

segments.speaker: david-sands
segments.translation: That is when I began owning hogs. When they grew up, then he gave me a boar. That was when they started having little ones. I had hogs for a long time. Then it ended. They closed the open range and I sold all the hogs.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: I tried it one time. I owned over 20 adults. Those red ones they call Durocs. In one year, they had litters and I owned over a hundred.

segments.speaker: david-sands
segments.translation: Oh, really, they would have eight or nine little ones.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Yes, mostly red ones, they were really a nuisance.

segments.speaker: david-sands
segments.translation: Truly. When that man gave me those, he would come back sometimes and buy some from me again, that man who gave them to me. He would come back and buy those little ones again. I did pretty good for a long time. If it was not for that, I would not have any clothes on. I was using the money to buy clothes.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: So that was really helpful to you?

segments.speaker: david-sands
segments.translation: I was buying shoes and pants.

segments.speaker: michael-cooksey
segments.translation: He might know what you were asking when they would throw them.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Yeah, that nobody has really told us good. You know when you kill a hog, how they throw its testicles in a tree.

segments.speaker: david-sands
segments.translation: Yes.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: What is the reason for that?

segments.speaker: david-sands
segments.translation: What was the reason for that? That was what my dad was getting on me about doing. They really did do that. I did see them doing that, when they fixed it all and removed the testicles. They would throw them in the tree. I guess it was... I don’t really know the reason.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: That is what we can’t find out. Nobody knows.

segments.speaker: david-sands
segments.translation: I guess you will own more hogs, I was thinking.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: They will raise a good litter?

segments.speaker: david-sands
segments.translation: They will raise a good litter, and the rest of it, is what I was thinking. I don’t know.

segments.speaker: michael-cooksey
segments.translation: When they hung them up, that meant something, ain’t it?

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Yes.

segments.speaker: michael-cooksey
segments.translation: But when they just hit, I don’t know.

segments.speaker: david-sands
segments.translation: Me too, but I have seen them doing that what he is talking about.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: What did you do to preserve that hog meat?

segments.speaker: david-sands
segments.translation: Back then we had a little building.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: They would call it a smoker.

segments.speaker: david-sands
segments.translation: They would put on a lot of salt.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: They would rub it on there.

segments.speaker: david-sands
segments.translation: The meat would just be white when Dad rubbed it on there. I guess that is what helped the meat, so nothing would happen to it. And for the ham, my dad, our neighbor had a smoker building, and he would take them there and smoke them. Then, when he would bring them back, he would hang them up in the smokehouse we called it. When my mom wanted meat, she would take a knife and go cut the meat and fry it. It was good.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: That is what I was thinking. I would have wanted that. I have seen just a little bit of that. My grandpa owned a lot of hogs. In the winter, and at Christmas, was when they killed those.

segments.speaker: david-sands
segments.translation: In the fall, when it starts to get cold, that was when Dad wanted to kill hogs.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Did y’all use all of the meat? The intestines, too?

segments.speaker: david-sands
segments.translation: Back then, the elders cleaned those intestines. I didn’t like them.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: You didn’t like them?

segments.speaker: david-sands
segments.translation: But I did like the meat. Mom made what they called hog head cheese from the head. I liked that, too.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: How long has it been since you ate that?

segments.speaker: david-sands
segments.translation: It’s been a long time since Mom...

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Nobody makes it now, ain’t it?

segments.speaker: david-sands
segments.translation: You can buy it at the store. But it’s not as good to me.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: It’s not as good.

segments.speaker: david-sands
segments.translation: It was not like how Mom would make it if Mom made it. I liked how Mom made it.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: I have not tried it.

segments.speaker: david-sands
segments.translation: It was good, to me.

segments.speaker: michael-cooksey
segments.translation: I like it, too.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: You liked it?

segments.speaker: michael-cooksey
segments.translation: Yeah, it’s greasy though. But I liked it.

segments.speaker: david-sands
segments.translation: That was good.

segments.speaker: michael-cooksey
segments.translation: How we lived a long time ago I have seen a little bit, too. No running water and helping butcher hogs. Nowadays, would you like to go back to how it was?

segments.speaker: david-sands
segments.translation: I would. Sometimes I think about it. I think I wished it was still like that. It was good. Things had a good taste. And going out into the woods and killing squirrels sometimes. And we would hunt coons for a long time. If I looked for young ones, I would kill them and I would clean them. I hung them up overnight.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: You would hang them up?

segments.speaker: david-sands
segments.translation: The next day I would clean them and get all the meat off. Then I would fry it.

segments.speaker: michael-cooksey
segments.translation: Then you fried it?

segments.speaker: david-sands
segments.translation: Barbecue.

segments.speaker: michael-cooksey
segments.translation: Did you sell those hides back then, too?

segments.speaker: david-sands
segments.translation: Yes, back then.

segments.speaker: michael-cooksey
segments.translation: About how much did they pay for them?

segments.speaker: david-sands
segments.translation: Yes, back then, a long time ago. We would sell them for 35 or 40 dollars. That’s how much one hide was worth.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: That was pretty good back then.

segments.speaker: david-sands
segments.translation: It was 35 or 45. And if it was big, it was 45, and the smaller ones were around 35. And if it was a bobcat, it was 80 or 90.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Was there more bobcats living back then?

segments.speaker: david-sands
segments.translation: Yes, we killed one or two all the time. We hunted every night. I had a good dog back then. He could tree coons. We killed three or four or five a night. And on Saturday mornings, we would go sell them. We made pretty good money then. We made about a hundred.

segments.speaker: michael-cooksey
segments.translation: Y’all did really live in a place where coons live on that big creek?

segments.speaker: david-sands
segments.translation: What do they call them? I was working on that ranch back then. Tom Tate’s ranch. I lived there on that ranch then. I could hunt everywhere back then. They called it Tulla Hollow.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: What is it?

segments.speaker: david-sands
segments.translation: Tulla Hollow was where we lived back then.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: That, what you are talking about, nowadays, if children were listening, there is not a doubt y’all had it hard, they would say, ain’t it?

segments.speaker: david-sands
segments.translation: Yes.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: What about you? Do you think y’all had it hard?

segments.speaker: david-sands
segments.translation: As for me, I don’t think so.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: That is what this one says.

segments.speaker: david-sands
segments.translation: I had two children, two girls back then. That was when I hunted coons. That was the money I used to buy gifts at Christmas to give to the children. From selling the coon hides.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: That is what this one says, and I do agree with him. He says we had it easier. The reason being is now, we pay for water. We didn’t use to buy it.

segments.speaker: david-sands
segments.translation: That is true, very true.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: And electricity.

segments.speaker: david-sands
segments.translation: For the last two or three months, I have begun buying water. I hooked it up to my house.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: That is what he says, but that is the way it is now. For those who are living now, if they could go back to where we were, they could not do it.

segments.speaker: david-sands
segments.translation: That is true.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: They could not do it.

segments.speaker: david-sands
segments.translation: Sometimes I think about that. A spring is better water to drink. There were about four or five springs in Pumpkin Hollow. Sometimes I would stop and get a drink.

segments.speaker: michael-cooksey
segments.translation: Are there still springs?

segments.speaker: david-sands
segments.translation: Yes.

segments.speaker: michael-cooksey
segments.translation: They still do? Where I come from, you can’t hardly find a spring.

segments.speaker: david-sands
segments.translation: There was one spring in Pumpkin Hollow that was good water to drink. And at Chewy on Proctor Road, a man hired me to do things all the time, to milk cows. He would hire me sometimes. He had good water coming out of his spring. It was extravagant to drink water from a place like that.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: What about in your past? What did you do for work?

segments.speaker: david-sands
segments.translation: When I began working, I pulled the weeds for farmers who were growing corn.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: You pulled the weeds around corn.

segments.speaker: david-sands
segments.translation: Different things like that, and fixing fences. When I started working, it was half a dollar an hour.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: You were getting paid.

segments.speaker: david-sands
segments.translation: When I started working, I worked a long time getting paid that much a day.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: That was four dollars a day.

segments.speaker: david-sands
segments.translation: Yes, I was making four dollars a day for a long time. Then one day, they added on a quarter.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: They added it on?

segments.speaker: david-sands
segments.translation: Then I was making three quarters a day.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Now you were getting rich.

segments.speaker: david-sands
segments.translation: Now I was making money then. Then one day, it became a dollar. For a long time, I worked for a dollar at that ranch, and then one day, it became two dollars and a quarter.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: I have seen a dollar and a quarter. I have seen it like that when I worked. I worked at Greenleaf. I was getting paid a dollar and a quarter an hour.

segments.speaker: david-sands
segments.translation: For a long time, he was paying me a dollar and a quarter an hour for a long time. Then it became two dollars and a quarter.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: When you said you like being in the woods, did y’all eat food from the woods?

segments.speaker: david-sands
segments.translation: Yes, Mom used different things that were green from the woods.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: So, it was just not onions and poke salad?

segments.speaker: david-sands
segments.translation: No, it wasn’t just onion and poke salad. It was different things.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Was it what they call kocheni?

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Do you like that?

segments.speaker: david-sands
segments.translation: Yes, it’s OK. As for me, I use a little bit of vinegar. I pour it on there, and it’s good.

segments.speaker: michael-cooksey
segments.translation: What about blueberry? Could you find it back then?

segments.speaker: david-sands
segments.translation: Yes, back then, that was all the elders looked for when blueberry was born.

segments.speaker: michael-cooksey
segments.translation: Can you still find it out that way nowadays?

segments.speaker: david-sands
segments.translation: I guess you can. It has been a year since I went to the woods. I knew where a lot used to grow. A gallon jug - just enough to get a cobbler made.

segments.speaker: michael-cooksey
segments.translation: That kind is hard to find.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Do you still do that? Go in the woods?

segments.speaker: david-sands
segments.translation: Sometimes, yes. I like going to the woods. I walk around in the woods sometimes.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: How old are you?

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: It doesn’t seem like it. You still walk around good.

segments.speaker: david-sands
segments.translation: I’m OK.

segments.speaker: michael-cooksey
segments.translation: He looks like he only 60, ain’t it?

segments.speaker: david-sands
segments.translation: What?

segments.speaker: michael-cooksey
segments.translation: You look like you are only 60.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: But the reason is you move around good.

segments.speaker: david-sands
segments.translation: It must be from fixing fences.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: You still do that.

segments.speaker: david-sands
segments.translation: Sometimes, or build new fences. Sometimes the farmers want fences fixed.

segments.speaker: michael-cooksey
segments.translation: There are lots of cattle owners that live out that way.

segments.speaker: david-sands
segments.translation: There are a lot that way. The Hamptons and also Vaughns, but mostly Hamptons.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Do those Hamptons still have horses to ride?

segments.speaker: david-sands
segments.translation: Sometimes.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Rodeo?

segments.speaker: david-sands
segments.translation: There is one, but he lives somewhere toward Siloam.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Oh, there somewhere.

segments.speaker: david-sands
segments.translation: The rest of them just raise cows. All those Hamptons have given me a job. I guess they raised me to work, the Hamptons. There were three elders - older men Hamptons. Chester Hampton, Wall Hampton, and Loyd Hampton. They would give me work all the time.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Is he the one that you said gave you those hogs?

segments.speaker: david-sands
segments.translation: Yes, one.

segments.speaker: michael-cooksey
segments.translation: Have you been on horseback a lot that way?

segments.speaker: david-sands
segments.translation: Not very much. I just worked on that ranch. I rode a horse sometimes when we would go get cows and bring them in.

segments.speaker: michael-cooksey
segments.translation: Could you rope?

segments.speaker: david-sands
segments.translation: No, just bring them in the corral.

segments.speaker: michael-cooksey
segments.translation: Did a horse ever buck you off?

segments.speaker: david-sands
segments.translation: No, I didn’t ride a horse very much. I just helped them sometimes to bring the cows into the corral.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: That was why I was saying I wouldn’t want to. A horse would have bucked me off somewhere there. Did your mom can things from the woods?

segments.speaker: david-sands
segments.translation: Yes, that kocheni I know of. They canned it and also poke salad.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: And onion, too?

segments.speaker: david-sands
segments.translation: No.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: She didn’t can it.

segments.speaker: david-sands
segments.translation: I never saw her do that, but poke salad and kocheni I did.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Were they cooked when she canned them?

segments.speaker: david-sands
segments.translation: Yes, and also... that is all that I know of. She grew some things like beans, too.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: She canned them.

segments.speaker: david-sands
segments.translation: Yes, and cucumbers, too.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: And also...?

segments.speaker: david-sands
segments.translation: And cabbage. Sauerkraut, she made.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Sauer – did she sometimes? I am not going to be able to say it.

segments.speaker: david-sands
segments.translation: Then she would be making blackberry jelly.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Oh, my wife makes that kind, too.

segments.speaker: david-sands
segments.translation: Also, like blueberry and that, too. Blueberry.

segments.speaker: michael-cooksey
segments.translation: There used to be wild plums that grew, too, ain’t it?

segments.speaker: david-sands
segments.translation: Yes, she would make jelly with that, too.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: That is very good.

segments.speaker: michael-cooksey
segments.translation: What about those kvnvtsi? Do you make them?

segments.speaker: david-sands
segments.translation: As for me, I don’t, but my mom and my brother used to make them. But now he doesn’t really do anything. Kvnvtsi is very good to drink. I don’t know who makes it now. I guess toward Stilwell there are a few living that make them.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: I make it.

segments.speaker: david-sands
segments.translation: My daughter bought it there. She works where they have that dialysis in Stilwell, that is where she works. There is one old lady that comes there who makes that kind.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Is it the kind that has things mixed in it or what? You could say like the hulls.

segments.speaker: david-sands
segments.translation: I guess so, I guess all of it.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: I take off the hulls.

segments.speaker: david-sands
segments.translation: Is that right, but a long time ago my mom...

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Would just grind it?

segments.speaker: david-sands
segments.translation: She would just grind, and what they call kvnoni, she would use one like that. But when she started, she would strain it.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: So it would not be mixed in there.

segments.speaker: david-sands
segments.translation: It would just be the juice. She would make the kvnvtsi from that.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: About September, we are going to start making it again. We still have a few hickory nuts.

segments.speaker: david-sands
segments.translation: Last year we picked up some hickory nuts. My wife’s sister was going to make some. She made it for a little while, but now I have not seen her make it. I don’t know what she used the hickory nuts I gave her for.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: We made over 80 last year.

segments.speaker: david-sands
segments.translation: That kind is very good.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: The Hamptons probably have quite a bit of land.

segments.speaker: david-sands
segments.translation: That is true. One of them has a huge amount of land. It starts all the way past Chewy. Where they say Clear Fork, it ends all the way over there, and where they call it New Hope, toward that way. He has all that land. And the Hamptons have that much, and then the Vaughns all the rest. I guess they have most of the land, the Hamptons and the Vaughns that own cows.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: And the Tates.

segments.speaker: david-sands
segments.translation: And the Tates have all of the development.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Oh, is that it?

segments.speaker: david-sands
segments.translation: This way in Pumpkin Hollow it’s all development toward the woods.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Have you been everywhere there where you are talking about?

segments.speaker: david-sands
segments.translation: Yes, I have gone everywhere in the woods when I worked at the ranch. I worked 15 years at that ranch there, and when I quit there, I worked in Adair County 22 years.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Were you driving a scraper (road grader)?

segments.speaker: david-sands
segments.translation: Yes.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Is that what you did?

segments.speaker: david-sands
segments.translation: Yes, for 15 years I scraped the roads.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: When you were in the woods, there is no doubt you found mushrooms.

segments.speaker: david-sands
segments.translation: Sometimes. I knew which ones they were. They called them unitlogi. They were yellow, this big [gesture]. There would be a lot of them, and then also wishi. Also, they get this tall [gesture].

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: What about?

segments.speaker: david-sands
segments.translation: And also white, the wanei (hickory chickens).

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Hickory chickens (they stick on a hickory).

segments.speaker: david-sands
segments.translation: They are good and white.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: What about deer horns they call them?

segments.speaker: david-sands
segments.translation: Deer horns yes, I have seen them, but they did not hardly live out that way.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: You have not eaten them?

segments.speaker: david-sands
segments.translation: No, but I have seen them. Where was it the last I saw those kind? I have not hardly seen those, but I have seen them sometimes.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Did you not know Rodger is his name? He is from Greasy.

segments.speaker: david-sands
segments.translation: Rodger Vann.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: He used to really go toward Chewy. He was a deacon at New Baptist, that one.

segments.speaker: david-sands
segments.translation: No, maybe I have seen him but I don’t know.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: His daughter told me about the deer horns. She said, “Man, I like them.” I did not know you could eat those kind.

segments.speaker: david-sands
segments.translation: They multiply, ain’t it, this tall [gesture].

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: They are like this [gesture].

segments.speaker: david-sands
segments.translation: I have seen them. Someone told me that those are good to eat.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: That is what she was telling me.

segments.speaker: david-sands
segments.translation: But that was the last time I saw them. I don’t see them anywhere anymore.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Did you find lots of wishi?

segments.speaker: david-sands
segments.translation: I know everywhere they grow. That boy, my daughter’s son, he found 14 on one tree. Some were that big [gesture], and some were this big [gesture]. He brought 14.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: One tree?

segments.speaker: david-sands
segments.translation: One. I said to him, “Where did you find all of those?” “I found all of them on one tree,” he said. “Man,” I said to him, “where at?” He told me, but he went there a year ago. “Grandpa,” he said to me, “that tree fell over. They are not stuck on there anymore.”

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: I am going to ask you something now, and if you want to keep it a secret, just say, “I am going to keep it a secret.” Are you related to Red?

segments.speaker: david-sands
segments.translation: I don’t know. They say we are brothers sometimes.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Well, he talks about it himself. One time, when I was pastoring at Twin Oaks, he was at the house. He also worked at the ranch. He said, “When we adjourn, stop by the house. I have some wishi and I will give y’all some,” he told us one time.

segments.speaker: david-sands
segments.translation: Oh, it was when he was working at that Blackfox ranch. Yes.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: So I stopped by. He had 28 on there.

segments.speaker: david-sands
segments.translation: They were finding them everywhere when my grandson was working there.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: He gave us eight this big [gesture]. Man, he had them scattered. That is what I was telling him, “Man, look how many you have scattered. You are just going to give me eight?”

segments.speaker: david-sands
segments.translation: He said he was selling them toward the last. When I talked to him. We talk sometimes, but not a lot.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: I guess he still goes to church at Twin Oaks.

segments.speaker: david-sands
segments.translation: Yes.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: And you are still at Chewy.

segments.speaker: david-sands
segments.translation: Yes.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Illinois River.

segments.speaker: david-sands
segments.translation: Tsisgvnigesdoi they call it in Cherokee.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Is that what they call it?

segments.speaker: david-sands
segments.translation: Tsisgvnigesdoi church.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: For the fish.

segments.speaker: david-sands
segments.translation: Tsisgvnigesdoi they call Illinois River in Cherokee.

segments.speaker: michael-cooksey
segments.translation: What kind of fish is that?

segments.speaker: david-sands
segments.translation: Carp.

segments.speaker: michael-cooksey
segments.translation: That’s it.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Who is that man that pastors y’all?

segments.speaker: david-sands
segments.translation: What?

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Who is that man that pastors y’all? What is his name?

segments.speaker: david-sands
segments.translation: James Wilkerson.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: James Wilkerson. Are my grandchildren still going to church?

segments.speaker: david-sands
segments.translation: Yeah, the children, they come every Sunday. We are going to baptize three on Sunday afternoon.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Oh, y’all are doing really good.

segments.speaker: david-sands
segments.translation: They are Russell.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: When y’all were growing up, when y’all got sick, did y’all know to go to the doctor, or did your parents or your grandpa know some medicine to use?

segments.speaker: david-sands
segments.translation: As for me, I don’t know nothing about that. But I do know they took us to the doctor when they could find someone to take us. We would come here in Tahlequah.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: You don’t remember anyone.

segments.speaker: david-sands
segments.translation: I know a little bit. They made something to drink for coughing. Things like that, I know from a long time ago. They would put a hole in a turtle and give us the blood. I don’t know, I guess it was for our coughing. It was medicine. I don’t know what it was.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Could it have been for the benefit of your heart?

segments.speaker: david-sands
segments.translation: I don’t know.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: This is the reason I am asking that. We were laying water lines at the house. I was the boss. Sometimes they call him a clean-up, that man that cleans, and we hired him. One would say, “Come to the house and we can eat there.” One time he said in the morning, “Come to the house. We will eat breakfast.” When I got there, he was already over there and he had it scattered. And when I looked good, it was those turtles you call them. He had them scattered out, and some he had already fixed. He said, “I want you to see this.” So that was up near what we call heart. It was doing this. When we got done eating, he said, “Stop back by in the evening.” So when I stopped back by in the evening, he said, “Let’s go look at what you looked at this morning.” In the evening, after five, it was still doing this.

segments.speaker: david-sands
segments.translation: The heart?

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Yes.

segments.speaker: david-sands
segments.translation: Turtle heart?

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Yes, it was still doing that. It was going. That is why I was thinking it was beneficial for that.

segments.speaker: david-sands
segments.translation: I guess it was. I don’t know. But I do know they gave us children the blood. I didn’t know the reason why, but they called it medicine.

segments.speaker: michael-cooksey
segments.translation: They would say that about a snake, too. I have heard that if you have killed it some time ago, its heart would still beat.

segments.speaker: david-sands
segments.translation: Yes, and a snake also. For a long time, it still does this. A snake does this for an hour or two hours after you have killed it. It still does this.

segments.speaker: michael-cooksey
segments.translation: A long time ago, I also heard them say that someone had swallowed a snake heart.

segments.speaker: david-sands
segments.translation: I don’t know.

segments.speaker: michael-cooksey
segments.translation: I have heard of it before.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: They were just crazy, but also if you cut a snake’s head off, with its head cut off it can still bite you.

segments.speaker: david-sands
segments.translation: Yes, they say it can still bite you. I don’t know, but I would not try it.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: That, you know, Frank Loyd?

segments.speaker: michael-cooksey
segments.translation: Yes.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: That is what happened to him. He had the head he had cut off sitting there. He was going to get it off, and it bit him here [gesture]. He took a picture of his hand. It was this big [gesture] and his skin was, what would you say? I forget how to say it now. He said that is what happened. He said he was going to get that head off, and he said it bit him.

segments.speaker: michael-cooksey
segments.translation: That is what happened to Tommy Carl, too, ain’t it?

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Yeah.

segments.speaker: michael-cooksey
segments.translation: And he was also permanently crippled. His whole arm. That kind is extremely bad.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: My grandchild, it was just a copperhead that bit him on his big toe. He laid in St. John’s for a week. Man, that cost us 274,000 dollars just to lay there for a week. One bottle of that liquid to give him a shot, it was just this big [gesture] 12 or 24, it was 12,000 dollars for one bottle of liquid to give him a shot with. I told him, “If it bites you a second time, you are just going to die.”

segments.speaker: michael-cooksey
segments.translation: What about the first time you got a car? What kind was it?

segments.speaker: david-sands
segments.translation: What?

segments.speaker: michael-cooksey
segments.translation: The first time you got a car, a big eyes. What kind was it?

segments.speaker: david-sands
segments.translation: Let me see, what kind was it? ‘49 Plymouth.

segments.speaker: michael-cooksey
segments.translation: How much did you pay for it?

segments.speaker: david-sands
segments.translation: It had one seat.

segments.speaker: michael-cooksey
segments.translation: It had one seat?

segments.speaker: michael-cooksey
segments.translation: How much did you pay for it, do you not remember?

segments.speaker: david-sands
segments.translation: Hundred, I think.

segments.speaker: michael-cooksey
segments.translation: Gah-lee.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Was it new?

segments.speaker: david-sands
segments.translation: What?

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Was it new?

segments.speaker: david-sands
segments.translation: No.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: It wasn’t, so it was used.

segments.speaker: david-sands
segments.translation: It was already several years old. I bought a ‘49 Plymouth the first time, and when several years had gone by, I would go to the peach harvest in Palisade, Colorado. I would go over there and we would pick peaches. We didn’t make very much. I brought back maybe a little over a hundred. When I came back to my house, I had 50 dollars. We went to Tahlequah. I looked for another car. A ‘53 Buick was the make there. It had forty-nine ninety-five on the windshield. We went by, I was looking all the way to the end of town for rubber tires, and when we went by, I said, “Wait, I want to go look at that Buick.” We looked at it, and I asked him, “Is that all you want?” He said, “Yes, forty-nine ninety-five.” That white man was telling me, “That is a good car.” He said, “Drive it.” I brought it to Tahlequah. I said, “OK, I will buy it.” And gave him 50 dollars. He gave me a nickel back. I had a nickel, but then I didn’t have any money to put gas in that car.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: So, you were able to fix things yourself back then.

segments.speaker: david-sands
segments.translation: Yes.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: It wasn’t anything like the computer, like it is nowadays.

segments.speaker: david-sands
segments.translation: No, that was all I gave him. When we went into the house, we wrote on a little paper, and then I signed. He gave me a nickel back and gave me the title. From Tahlequah, I headed back toward Chewy driving a Buick.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Was it a standard?

segments.speaker: david-sands
segments.translation: Yeah, it was kind of a standard. I don’t know what they called them.

segments.speaker: michael-cooksey
segments.translation: They had them here to change the gears.

segments.speaker: david-sands
segments.translation: I would be going 40 or 50 [miles per hour]. I would put it in low gear like I was sitting still. Boy, they called them straight-eights. It had a motor like that in there. We drove it for a long time.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: About how old were you then?

segments.speaker: david-sands
segments.translation: 21 or 22, something like that, then.

segments.speaker: michael-cooksey
segments.translation: Did you drive that toward Colorado?

segments.speaker: david-sands
segments.translation: No, not hardly. Someone would take us.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Where they cut broom corn, have you been there?

segments.speaker: david-sands
segments.translation: Yes, Mom and Dad, we all went. The whole family would live there as one where they call it, Walsh, Colorado. We would get there. There was an elder that lived there. I don’t know what kind of house it was. We lived there and there was another building. Mom and another old woman from Colcord became the cooks there. And Dad and that woman’s husband got together and cooked something to eat. We were doing good living there in Walsh, Colorado.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Did y’all get paid by the hour?

segments.speaker: david-sands
segments.translation: I don’t know how much it was. I don’t think it was very much.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Are they tall?

segments.speaker: david-sands
segments.translation: They are. You had to look up. The rows are half a mile long. I was cutting five a day. I was cutting five rows.

segments.speaker: michael-cooksey
segments.translation: Five rows?

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Half a mile. Were some pretty quick?

segments.speaker: david-sands
segments.translation: Yeah, some were. John Deer, Track Jones, and Sqwan was his name. He grew up in the family. John Mvtiski. They were really...

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Were quick.

segments.speaker: david-sands
segments.translation: They were quick at cutting it, and if they were quick at cutting it, they paid them more. They would cut more rows. Somewhere around six times, I went doing that every year.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: So when y’all cut it, did y’all just lay them there on the ground?

segments.speaker: david-sands
segments.translation: Yes, they called it ‘down row’. They would give us five rows. The boss would give us five rows, and the middle was the down row. You can pull with your hand and cut them, and put them on this side. Then we would gather them up. We would do the same with the others and make down rows. There would be a lot, and when you cut five, it would be piled up over there [gesture]. And when you’re all done, they bring a long sled with a tractor and put them on there.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Different one would do that?

segments.speaker: david-sands
segments.translation: Yes, that was a big machine that took off the seed. I guess they made brooms from the stems. I don’t know what they did with them, but it went through the machine.

segments.speaker: michael-cooksey
segments.translation: It got the seed off.

segments.speaker: david-sands
segments.translation: They made seed.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Did you like going over there?

segments.speaker: david-sands
segments.translation: It was OK, I liked it. But on the weekend, what they called pheasants, we looked for them. We would kill them.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: They allowed y’all to?

segments.speaker: david-sands
segments.translation: Yeah, there. All of it.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: In fields, do you like that kind of meat?

segments.speaker: david-sands
segments.translation: Yes, it’s good.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Oh yeah, it’s good ain’t it?

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Have you ate a pheasant?

segments.speaker: michael-cooksey
segments.translation: No.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Oh it’s really good.

segments.speaker: david-sands
segments.translation: They will be out there like chickens.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: As for me, I liked that pheasant more than I did chicken.

segments.speaker: david-sands
segments.translation: My dad had a pickup and we would drive that on weekends. They be just like chickens everywhere. We would choose the males and kill the males.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: How can you tell if it is a male?

segments.speaker: david-sands
segments.translation: It has a long tail. It is black, and the head is brown. The males are kind of red, and also here [gesture] it will be red.

segments.speaker: michael-cooksey
segments.translation: They are a pretty color, ain’t it?

segments.speaker: david-sands
segments.translation: They have pretty tails.

segments.speaker: michael-cooksey
segments.translation: When I was little, I had some. Two males and three females. Someone gave them to Steve, and I had them penned up and was feeding them. I don’t know what happened.

segments.speaker: david-sands
segments.translation: I raised them for a little while, those pheasants, but they were not doing too good. So, I just quit.

segments.speaker: michael-cooksey
segments.translation: They got out on me. That was the last time I saw them.

segments.speaker: david-sands
segments.translation: They got out on me, too.

segments.speaker: michael-cooksey
segments.translation: They are wild, ain’t it?

segments.speaker: david-sands
segments.translation: I didn’t see them a second time. I don’t know what happened to them when they got out. That was the last.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: That’s a little bit like my son that lives in Kansas. When I had cows, he wanted a cow, too, and he saved to buy him a cow. I brought him to Stilwell and he bought one. So, when we took it back, we put it in the lot. Just when we let it go, it went over the fence. It went over two fences - he was like this [expression] looking at it. We never did find that cow. I felt sorry for him, but also it was funny. He was watching it go over.

segments.speaker: michael-cooksey
segments.translation: What about nowadays? Are you retired from working, or do you still do things?

segments.speaker: david-sands
segments.translation: I just do different things, like what I was telling you a while ago. I still build fences.

segments.speaker: michael-cooksey
segments.translation: They still hire you sometimes.

segments.speaker: david-sands
segments.translation: Sometimes, but for now, I mostly cut grass.

segments.speaker: michael-cooksey
segments.translation: So, you still move around pretty good.

segments.speaker: david-sands
segments.translation: OK, and also sometimes someone will call me to cut grass and weedeat.

segments.speaker: michael-cooksey
segments.translation: Do you have one of those?

segments.speaker: david-sands
segments.translation: Yes, a steer. For a long time, I just had one of those little ones. Then my nephew - it was my grandson, said, “Grandpa, get you one of them zero turns,” he said to me. I said someone would find me down in a ravine. He said, “No, it is easy to do.” So finally, I got one. And below my house, you can get on it and try it, my grandson told me. I was playing with it, and that was when I started. That kind is good, especially if you have to cut a lot in a big place. You would not take very long.

segments.speaker: michael-cooksey
segments.translation: When I first tried it, I had never ridden one before.

segments.speaker: david-sands
segments.translation: Me either.

segments.speaker: michael-cooksey
segments.translation: I got one, and got it off, but I could not go straight. Not until I got used to driving around.

segments.speaker: david-sands
segments.translation: It was easy then.

segments.speaker: michael-cooksey
segments.translation: Then I started cutting.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: They were telling me to get off, we are going to finish in a little bit. You are a deacon, right?

segments.speaker: david-sands
segments.translation: Yes.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: How long have you been a deacon?

segments.speaker: david-sands
segments.translation: Three years. I was a trainee and then in 1979...

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: You were looked at.

segments.speaker: david-sands
segments.translation: I was looked at in 1979, and that’s when I began as deacon at Illinois River Church. I have been a deacon there all the time since then.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: That is over 50 years, then.

segments.speaker: david-sands
segments.translation: It has been a long time. That is where I started going to church. Dad and Mom were going to church then. That was when I started going there, but for a long time I was just going there until I started making mistakes in the world. The boys started looking for me. We were making mistakes. That is when I thought, it is best if I just stop doing bad. I started praying. It was probably '62 or '63 when I started going to church, and in ‘68 or ‘69 I guess, then I surrendered.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: And you have been in there since then.

segments.speaker: david-sands
segments.translation: Yes.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Just where you started.

segments.speaker: david-sands
segments.translation: Then one day they chose me as a trainee deacon. I trained for two or three years. Raymond Glass was our pastor then.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Did not Sanders test you?

segments.speaker: david-sands
segments.translation: Let’s see, who was it? I don’t know, it might have been him. Joe Pasheka was one of them.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Joe lived nearby, ain’t it?

segments.speaker: david-sands
segments.translation: Yes, and also Raymond who was the other. There were four of them, I think. Sqwan was one of them.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Yes, that is Sanders.

segments.speaker: david-sands
segments.translation: They tested me then.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Did you get baptized there at that river?

segments.speaker: david-sands
segments.translation: Yes.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Is that where y’all baptize when it is good?

segments.speaker: david-sands
segments.translation: Yes, Illinois River.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: OK, we are going to finish up now. But what us Cherokee believe, from time to time you might have heard them talking, or you may have seen what we call tsigili. Nothing like that has ever scared you if you saw it?

segments.speaker: david-sands
segments.translation: As for me, I have not. We lived on Proctor Road. All the Cherokee talked about little people on the road. Where we lived, in the evening, when I didn’t have a car, us boys and teenagers would meet at Chewy all the time. We would go everywhere and would meet at Chewy store. I would leave and go walk over there in the evenings. About one or two o’clock at night, I would go back toward the house. As for me, I never saw or heard anything like that.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: You probably were not even thinking about it, were you?

segments.speaker: david-sands
segments.translation: No, I have never thought about anything like that, but when I grew up, Walt O Wall was his name, he came to the house sometimes when he was drinking at nighttime. He would lay outside on the porch when he came, never in the house. He would just lay there. We were talking, and he said, “Some little people went by this morning.” I said to him, “What is that?” He said, “They are just little people. They were talking when they went by.” As for me, I have never heard anything like that.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: You have not seen them either?

segments.speaker: david-sands
segments.translation: No, I would go everywhere. I never did, and those tsigilis they were seeing, as for me, I had never seen anything. And I have been in the woods a lot. In the woods, what they call Bigfoot or something, I was telling them I have never seen anything like that. But I have seen hogs in the woods, and also deer and coyotes and foxes and different things.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Did you see any bear?

segments.speaker: david-sands
segments.translation: No, I never saw a bear, but saw everything else being in the woods. A year went by, I was walking around in the woods. I have never seen anything like that. But different things like deer or hogs and squirrels and different things I saw.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: What about those hogs you are talking about that live in the woods? Did you kill them from time to time?

segments.speaker: david-sands
segments.translation: What?

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Did you kill them sometimes?

segments.speaker: david-sands
segments.translation: Yes, we killed them sometimes. That is good meat to eat.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: I liked it.

segments.speaker: david-sands
segments.translation: It has been over five years now. I think we killed 14 in Pumpkin Hollow. Tom Tate’s child lived there. They let us kill hogs. There are a lot that live there in the woods. We went at nighttime and killed them. We would clean them at the house and get the backstrap. Really, the boys started eating it up when we got something.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: We would trap them. We trapped 13 of them, and they were just this big [gesture], but we did fix them.

segments.speaker: david-sands
segments.translation: Yes, they are good to eat. Man, that is good eating. The boys really like it when they kill one. We don’t have the meat very long. They eat it up. They cook it when they come back from school. They cook it theirselves them boys, when they want something like that. We don’t have meat very long. They eat it up quickly.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: What about your parents or grandpa or your grandma? Have they ever mentioned how the Cherokee were brought out from old Cherokee and Georgia?

segments.speaker: david-sands
segments.translation: I have not hardly heard of it. On my dad’s side, his mother is the only one I know. She was blind, as I was telling you earlier. That is the only one I know that went out to where we live. And on my mom’s side, she was a Reese, my mother. I have not hardly heard anything.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Joe Reese, is that a relative?

segments.speaker: david-sands
segments.translation: That was her that was Joe Reese’s aunt. Joe Reese’s Dad, that was her brother.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: I am going to ask you this last. This Cherokee that we are talking, what do you think is going to happen to it?

segments.speaker: david-sands
segments.translation: I really don’t know. I wish it wouldn’t go out. It probably will one day, unless these learners learn it good. And it will keep going. I hope it does.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: I am thankful you came.

segments.speaker: david-sands
segments.translation: I am thankful, too.
